items.title: Live Updates: Extreme Heat and Strong Winds Fuel Wildfires in France and Spain
items.summary: Firefighters are tackling new blazes while others have been contained, and hundreds of thousands of people have been forced to flee. A new heat wave forecast to hit Europe could make conditions worse.

items.title: Israeli settlers set fire to mosques, cars and farm land in West Bank, Palestinians say
items.summary: The latest attacks come two days after a clash between settlers and Palestinians near the village of Tell, which left four Palestinians and two Israelis dead.

items.title: Berlin Police Search for Suspect in Fatal Attack on Pride Parade
items.summary: The hunt for a 21-year-old man with links to local Islamic groups began early Sunday. The police said they were investigating the attack as a possible act of terrorism.

items.title: Senate candidate Josh Turek handcycles the Iowa campaign trail
items.summary: State Representative Josh Turek, the Democrat running to flip Iowa’s open Senate seat, cycled with his hands at an Iowa biking event that took place between two cities nearly 60 miles apart.

items.title: U.S.-Iran War Pauses for 2nd Straight Day
items.summary: President Trump put off plans to escalate the fighting in part because of dwindling stockpiles of interceptor missiles, American officials said.

items.title: What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack
items.summary: A police manhunt is underway after a suspect rammed a car into a crowd at a Pride event in the German capital on Saturday night.

items.title: France battles fire 'whirlwinds' as another 55,000 evacuated
items.summary: More than 340,000 people have now been evacuated from wildfires in France and Spain.

Burnham’s comments came as Wes Streeting, the new defence secretary, said he did not believe the Trump administration was looking for allies who “suck up”, but rather those with the confidence to set out disagreements when needed. items.summary: In some cases, no direct line can be drawn from the president’s domestic nuclear agenda to his family or close allies. But they have overlapping business ties that could position them for gains.

items.title: Trump Seems Trapped by Iran War, Even as He Wields the World’s Biggest Hammer
items.summary: A president who thought there were no limits to his power has discovered several, leaving him more frustrated and erratic.

items.title: Democrats Reset the Maine Senate Race. Now Comes the Tricky Part.
items.summary: Troy Jackson is replacing Graham Platner, but Republicans are seeking to tie them together as a remade race kicks off with high stakes.

items.title: Inside the Phone-Throwing Drama at the Troubled, Broke Democratic Party
items.summary: The Democrats should be well positioned to make gains in this year’s midterms. But inside party headquarters, every week brings paranoia, worries about money and, on occasion, emotional eruptions.

items.title: Employers Fear Labor Shortage as Many Immigrants Lose Protected Status
items.summary: A recent Supreme Court ruling cleared the way for the Trump administration to end a humanitarian program that has allowed about one million immigrants to work legally in the U.S.

items.title: E.U. Divided Over Barring Imports From Israeli Settlements
items.summary: The discussion about restricting goods from Israeli settlements in occupied territories reflects a European split over whether and how to confront Israel.

items.title: Birmingham council accused of giving ‘free rein’ to group erecting England flags
items.summary: Campaigners call for injunction against Raise the Colours, which is accused of spreading anti-immigration rhetoric Birmingham residents have accused the local council and police of “dragging their heels” and giving “free rein” to a group responsible for erecting flags across the city. Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, has been placing union jack and St George’s cross flags on lamp-posts, roundabouts and other public infrastructure since last summer. items.title: Family of former Vodafone manager found drowned call for ‘Adrian’s law’ to protect franchisees
items.summary: Adrian Howe’s family believe that fears his deal would be financially ruinous led him to kill himself The family of a former mobile phone store manager who was found drowned days before his new Vodafone franchise was to open its doors is pressing the government to introduce a new franchising law in his name. The call comes a week after Vodafone settled a long-running legal claim filed by 62 of its former franchisees who alleged that the company “unjustly enriched”…

items.title: UK journalists ‘self-censoring stories about Trump and the right over safety fears’
items.summary: Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’ Journalists are self-censoring their reporting on rightwing protests, Donald Trump’s administration and trans issues because of growing concerns about their personal safety, with newsrooms accused of “normalising” the risks they face. Hundreds of journalists from across the UK have anonymously disclosed increasing nervousness over their security. items.title: Venezuela men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jail
items.summary: Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown Venezuelan men sent last year to a notorious Salvadorian terrorism prison by the Trump administration are suing the US aviation companies that transported them there. items.title: 20 Years After Its Own Outbreak, an Ugandan Town Beats Back Ebola
items.summary: The Bundibugyo Ebola virus takes its name from this small town, where it was first discovered in 2007. Now, the species has returned to eastern Congo, halting life on a busy border.
